message.reasoning:
I need to decide on an auction bid for Marvin Gardens.

I cannot bid $101 because I only have $99 cash. I must drop out.

p1 raised the bid to $100. They can afford it with $138 cash, leaving them with only $38. That is too little for a $150 Indiana house. They own an unmortgaged red monopoly.

p1 cannot mortgage their red properties to fund a house because those streets already have houses. They would be overpaying for Marvin Gardens, which is worth only $140 in mortgage value.

p1 likely raised the bid to $100 to deny me and split the yellow set. Dropping out is the only legal option. I am now recalculating p1's cash to verify whether they can still afford an Indiana house.

p1 cannot build an Indiana house regardless of the auction outcome. Even winning at $39 would leave them with $99, still short of the $150 needed. They own no unmortgaged non-developed properties to mortgage, and their red streets already have houses.

I am now calculating the rent returns for a 4/4/4 light blue set. If I had won at $40, I would have $59 cash and could mortgage Marvin for $140 to reach $199 total. Building fourth houses on all three streets costs $150, leaving me with $49. I am checking standard Monopoly rent values for Oriental, Vermont, and Connecticut.

Standard Monopoly rent values confirm a 4/4/4 light blue set would yield $400, $400, and $450. I cannot bid $101, so I must drop out. p1's jump to $100 denied me the property and drained their cash to $38, leaving them vulnerable.
